title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Atlanta, GA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Atlanta: towers and data halls, aerospace and airline work, power plants, Georgia DOT bridges and pipelines. Online or on site.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Atlanta: A Six-Day Course for Georgia's Construction, Aerospace, Power and Manufacturing Inspectors
html:
Atlanta grew up as a rail junction and became the commercial capital of the Southeast, and it still builds at a pace few cities match. Cranes over Midtown, data halls on the metro's edge, hangars at the world's busiest passenger airport, power plants run from a corporate headquarters downtown, and car plants a short drive down the interstates all depend on welded steel. Somebody has to sign off on those welds, and Georgia contracts keep naming the AWS Certified Welding Inspector for that job. Atlanta-area welders, fitters, QC inspectors, NDT technicians and engineers can prepare for the AWS examination with Atlantis NDT's CWI exam-prep course, a six-day (6-day) program organized around Fundamentals, Practical and Code Application.

The certificate on the wall will come from AWS, not from Atlantis. The American Welding Society controls eligibility, administers all three exam parts, scores them and certifies the candidates who pass. This course carries no AWS approval or endorsement, and Atlantis has no window into the examination itself. For the full syllabus and the exam structure AWS publishes, read the national AWS CWI exam prep course page. What follows is about Georgia.

Building the Atlanta skyline, one connection at a time

Commercial construction is the biggest single source of CWI work in metro Atlanta. Office and residential towers in Midtown and Buckhead, hospital expansions, university buildings, logistics warehouses along I-75 and I-85, and the convention, sports and entertainment venues downtown all use structural steel. Georgia adopts the International Building Code as part of its State Minimum Standard Codes, maintained by the Department of Community Affairs, and local building departments enforce it. On many permitted projects that means special inspection of structural welding by an inspector working for the owner.

Those inspectors mostly work for geotechnical, materials testing and inspection firms headquartered or branched in the metro. Their day involves verifying welder qualifications, checking joint fit-up and preheat, measuring fillet sizes and groove reinforcement, and comparing each finished weld with AWS D1.1, the structural welding code for steel. Fabricators supplying those projects, many of them in the suburbs and in smaller Georgia towns, need their own CWIs for shop quality control. If that is your world, D1.1 is the obvious Part C book; read the summary of the structural steel code, then work through how D1.1 accepts or rejects a weld.

Data centers on the metro's edge

Over the last few years metro Atlanta has turned into one of the fastest-growing data-center markets in the country, with large campuses rising in the counties west and south of the city and along the northern suburbs. Each campus is a welding project dressed as a technology project: steel building frames and equipment platforms, chilled-water and condenser piping, fuel systems for backup generators, and steel structures in the electrical yard. Mechanical contractors, steel erectors and the testing agencies that serve them all hire inspectors who can move between a structural weld in the morning and a piping weld after lunch.

That mix raises the Part C question early. A candidate who spends most hours on the mechanical side, where welders are qualified under ASME Section IX and the piping is built to one of the B31 codes, may do better with the ASME selection than with D1.1. The Section IX summary explains how ASME treats procedure and welder qualification.

Aircraft, airlines and aerospace suppliers

Aerospace is the second pillar of north Georgia's welding economy. Lockheed Martin builds military transport aircraft at its plant in Marietta, northwest of the city, and Delta Air Lines runs a major maintenance, repair and overhaul operation at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. Around both sit machine shops, ground-support equipment makers, tooling builders and component suppliers.

Aerospace welding inspection works differently from structural inspection. Flight hardware is welded and inspected to customer and military specifications, and AWS D17.1, the specification for fusion welding in aerospace applications, is the AWS document most closely tied to that work and one of the Part C options. Airline maintenance, meanwhile, runs under FAA regulations and the carrier's own maintenance program, and a CWI does not authorize anyone to return an aircraft part to service. For an inspector in a supplier's weld shop, though, the CWI is a recognized, portable credential that makes the aerospace-specific qualification easier to build on. For the NDT side of this sector, see ultrasonic testing in aviation and aviation NDT training.

Power generation and the Georgia grid

Georgia Power, part of Atlanta-headquartered Southern Company, operates a fleet of coal, gas, hydro and nuclear plants across the state, and the completion of two new reactors at Plant Vogtle near Waynesboro made Georgia's nuclear construction story national news. Power plants generate steady inspection work during outages and modifications: boiler tube repairs, power piping, structural supports, pressure-retaining components and the steel structures in switchyards and substations.

Power piping is built to ASME B31.1, with procedures and welders qualified under Section IX, so plant-side candidates often lean toward the ASME selection for Part C. One limit should be stated clearly: nuclear safety-related work is governed by the plant owner's nuclear quality assurance program, and Atlantis does not provide nuclear quality-assurance services. The CWI is relevant to many non-nuclear and balance-of-plant jobs, but the nuclear program decides who inspects safety-related welds. Related NDT reading: ultrasonic testing in power generation and magnetic particle testing in power plants.

Factories along I-85 and I-16

Georgia has pulled in large manufacturing investments over two decades, many of them automotive. Kia builds vehicles at its plant in West Point, on the Alabama line southwest of Atlanta, and Hyundai Motor Group has opened a large electric-vehicle plant near Savannah. Each anchor plant brings dozens of suppliers stamping, welding and assembling parts in towns along the interstates. Add trailer and truck-body builders, agricultural and construction equipment makers, tank fabricators and steel service centers, and the state has a deep base of production welding.

Automotive production welding is mostly robotic resistance and arc welding with its own industry standards, and those standards are not CWI Part C books. Yet the plants still employ welding engineers and quality staff who use the credential to show broad competence, and the suppliers that build structural frames, conveyors and tooling for the plants work to D1.1. A welder who started on a robotic line and moved into maintenance or quality often has the kind of varied experience the CWI rewards.

Bridges, interchanges and pipelines across Georgia

The Georgia Department of Transportation and local agencies keep a steady flow of bridge and interchange work moving through the metro and the rest of the state. Steel bridge members are fabricated and inspected to AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, plus the owner's special provisions, which tighten procedure and consumable control and add fracture control requirements for critical members. Inspectors who want to work for bridge fabricators or GDOT's inspection consultants should consider D1.5 for Part C; the AWS D1.5 overview explains how it is laid out.

Pipelines run through the state as well. Colonial Pipeline, which carries refined fuels from the Gulf Coast toward the Northeast, has its headquarters in the Atlanta suburb of Alpharetta, and gas distribution utilities serve the metro's huge customer base. Steel pipeline welding is qualified and accepted under API 1104 in most of that work, which makes it the natural Part C book for pipeline and utility inspectors. The API 1104 summary walks through its sections.

Georgia's technical colleges and the AWS Atlanta Section

Most Georgia welders learn the trade in the Technical College System of Georgia. Atlanta Technical College, on the south side of the city, offers a Welding and Joining Technology diploma covering stick welding in flat, horizontal, vertical and overhead positions plus MIG, flux-cored and TIG work, with a course aimed at preparing students for industrial qualification tests. West Georgia Technical College, whose LaGrange campus serves the corridor around the Kia plant, received an AWS Foundation Welding Workforce Grant, and officers of the AWS Atlanta Section visited its welding lab in February 2022 to recognize the grant and encourage students to form an AWS student chapter. Other technical colleges ring the metro, and building-trades apprenticeships give ironworkers, boilermakers and pipefitters a paid path into welding.

The Atlanta Section is the local arm of AWS for the metro. Its outreach to schools, scholarship promotion and meetings give candidates a chance to talk with working inspectors about the practical exam and about which firms are hiring. Check the AWS section directory on aws.org for current meeting details.

None of these programs leads directly to the CWI. AWS wants years of documented, verifiable welding-related work first, and the required number shrinks as relevant education grows: a candidate with a high school diploma needs five years, and the full scale appears on the national course page. Keep your technical college transcript, because a completed trade or vocational program can count toward a year of the requirement.

Scheduling the examination from Atlanta

After AWS accepts an application it sends a confirmation with an eligibility code, and that code is what lets you book Fundamentals and Code Application, both computer-based, at a Prometric testing center. Metro Atlanta has several. The practical stands apart: AWS gives it only at selected venues linked to its seminars, on a calendar AWS sets, and candidates evaluate specimens with gauges and documents AWS supplies. Look up the nearest practical venue on aws.org before mapping out study, since that date is the hardest one to move.

Clearing the bar means scoring 72% or higher on Fundamentals, the Practical and Code Application alike, with the three results returned together. A vision examination on the current AWS form, covering close-range acuity and color perception, is also part of the application. Exam charges belong to AWS and are listed on its site; for travel, books and the rest of the budget, see the CWI exam budget planner. To understand where candidates lose points, read CWI results part by part.

How the six days work for Atlanta candidates

Whether you study alone or with coworkers, the content runs in the same order. The first two days build Part A knowledge: welding and cutting processes, AWS terminology, joint configurations and welding symbols, followed by base-metal and weld-metal behavior, mechanical tests, the root causes of common discontinuities, the NDT methods a welding inspector calls for, safety and professional ethics. Day three rehearses the practical: gauge reading, profile measurement and visual judgment against a written set of requirements. Day four is spent navigating the candidate's chosen code. Day five puts all three parts under timed conditions, and day six revisits the topics those mock papers flagged before closing with an exam-day plan and a checklist of application documents.

Self-paced, with an instructor on call

Individual candidates follow the course online. You receive a plan that spreads the six days across your own calendar, reading material, practice items Atlantis authored from the public topic outline, mock papers with time limits, and access to an instructor for questions. Commuters on the Connector, outage workers and second-shift welders can all fit it in, because nothing is timetabled. None of the practice material reproduces AWS examination content.

On site for an Atlanta employer

A testing firm, fabricator, mechanical contractor or plant can host the program at its own location for a group of employees over six days. The hands-on preparation then uses the company's measuring tools and welds cut from its own work, and code practice concentrates on the book the team actually uses. Applications still go to AWS one person at a time, and each candidate has to satisfy the experience and vision rules personally.

Adding NDT methods in Georgia

A CWI's main tools are the eye, the gauge and the code. When a weld needs to be checked below the surface or for fine surface cracks, the job passes to NDT technicians. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, their own employer certifies them once they have completed classroom hours, logged method experience and passed its examinations. Atlanta CWIs who add ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant testing widen the work they can take on, from bridge members to power piping. Atlantis offers SNT-TC-1A-based courses for those methods: see NDT training in Atlanta, NDT training in Georgia, ultrasonic testing in Atlanta, magnetic particle testing in Atlanta and penetrant testing in Atlanta. Visual technique improves with VT Level 1 training; inspection steps can be rehearsed in a browser in the welding workshop simulator; and method knowledge can be checked with free practice tests.

Once certified, track the dates. Under AWS rules the CWI covers a nine-year span, and renewal forms are due when the third and sixth years come around, with full recertification at the end of the ninth. AWS also expects a current vision record when you renew. For the bigger career picture, see CWI requirements and career impact.

Asking for a quote from Atlanta

Give us the number of candidates, a brief summary of each person's schooling and welding background, the Part C code each one expects to choose, and whether anyone has already applied to AWS or booked a practical. For a group at your site, include the address, the gauges and sample welds available, and the weeks that suit your production or project calendar. The Atlanta request form is the quickest route; we reply within one business day.

Other Southeast cities: CWI exam prep in Charlotte, Nashville and Jacksonville.

faq.q: Can I take the course at an Atlanta training center?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlanta site; Atlantis operates from Houston and Hyderabad. Georgia candidates study online with instructor help, or a company runs the full program at its plant or office for its staff. See the course outline.

faq.q: Does finishing the course make me a CWI?
faq.a: No. AWS administers the examination and grants the certification. The course readies you for the three parts, but the AWS eligibility review, the vision examination and the exam itself are still ahead of you.

faq.q: Which code book should an Atlanta special inspector choose?
faq.a: AWS D1.1, because building steel across Georgia is judged against it. See the D1.1 overview.

faq.q: I weld in an aerospace supplier's shop in Marietta. Which Part C option fits?
faq.a: AWS D17.1, the aerospace fusion welding specification, is the closest match. Remember that flight hardware also follows customer and military specifications.

faq.q: Does a CWI let me inspect safety-related welds at a nuclear plant?
faq.a: Not by itself. Nuclear safety-related work follows the plant owner's nuclear quality assurance program, which decides who inspects. Atlantis does not provide nuclear quality-assurance services.

faq.q: I graduated from a Georgia technical college welding program. Am I eligible?
faq.a: Not yet, unless you also have the required years of documented welding-related work. A completed trade or vocational program can reduce the requirement, but AWS still expects verified experience.

faq.q: Where will I sit the exam?
faq.a: Fundamentals and Code Application are computer-based tests at Prometric centers in the metro. The practical happens only at AWS-selected venues on AWS dates; check aws.org for the closest one.
AWS lists a minimum of 72% on each of the three parts, reported together once all are complete.

faq.q: Are the practice questions copied from the AWS exam?
faq.a: No. Atlantis wrote them from the topic outline AWS publishes, and it has no access to the real examination.

faq.q: How do I find the AWS Atlanta Section?
faq.a: Use the section directory on aws.org. The Atlanta Section visits schools, promotes AWS Foundation scholarships and holds meetings where you can meet working inspectors.
Each request is quoted individually. AWS posts its exam charges on its own site, and the budget planner covers the other costs. Request a quote.
